extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors/writers who may pitch literary agents in person
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting and delivering a tight, well-rehearsed 30-second (elevator) pitch to literary agents that introduces the writer, states the goal, shows relevant qualifications, and ends with a call to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the literary agent who you are
rubrics_metrics.description: State your name and job title, or the title of the position you’re seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “Hi, my name is Miranda Mechanic, and I’m a licensed automotive mechanic who writes how-to articles for women who don’t want their cars to get the best of them.” Keep this succinct so the agent immediately knows who you are and your relevant identity/role.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what you want
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t beat around the bush. State what you’re after (your objective) clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “I’m interested in placing some of my articles with your magazine, Auto Care for Everybody.” Being direct about your goal helps the agent understand whether they can help and prevents wasted time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the literary agent why you’re the best choice
rubrics_metrics.description: List any degrees, writing credentials, training or experience that relate to what you’re seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sure the qualifications match your stated goal — mismatched credentials (e.g., degrees in an unrelated field) won’t help. If you lack related experience, name qualities or skills (attention to detail, passion, etc.). The key is to be brief and memorable and to highlight that special something separating you from the crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give literary agents a call to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude by asking for what you want or offering a next step to prompt further interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “I’d like to show you copies of my articles, including ‘How to Change a Tire When It’s Twenty Below Zero’ ...” The call to action leads to further interaction — do not neglect this step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the pitch very short, tight, and well-rehearsed (30 seconds or fewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare to pitch your idea in 30 seconds or fewer (this is called an “Elevator Pitch”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a tight, well-rehearsed pitch and commit it to memory so you don’t waste an opportunity. The piece is meant as a sound-byte; practice to make it smooth and concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor the pitch to the agent/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt the content and emphasis of your few key sentences to the type of agent (market/location/genre) you’re addressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether you’re pitching to New York or London literary agents, children’s or Christian literary agents, top-ranking or new agents, craft sentences that fit their focus. Targeting increases the chance the agent will be interested.
